title: Current-Voltage Relations: Ohmic and Non-Ohmic Resistance
topicTitle: Current-voltage relations; ohmic and non-ohmic resistance
notes: Ohm's Law: For an ohmic conductor at constant physical conditions (especially temperature), the current $I$ flowing through it is directly proportional to the potential difference $V$ across its ends: $V = IR$, where $R$ is the resistance. The graph of $V$ vs $I$ is a straight line through the origin.

Resistance Definition: Resistance $R$ of a conductor is defined as the ratio of potential difference across it to the current through it: $R = V/I$. SI unit: ohm ($\Omega = 	ext{V/A} = 	ext{V}^2/	ext{W}$). Dimensions: $[M L^2 T^{-3} I^{-2}]$.

Resistivity: The resistance of a uniform conductor depends on its geometry and material: $R = \rho L/A$, where $\rho$ is resistivity (material property), $L$ is length, and $A$ is cross-sectional area. SI unit of $\rho$: $\Omega\cdot	ext{m}$. Conductivity $\sigma = 1/\rho$.

Ohmic Conductors: Conductors that obey Ohm's law ($V$-$I$ graph is linear) are called ohmic. Examples: metals at constant temperature, electrolytes, carbon resistors. Their resistance is independent of $V$ and $I$ (within limits).

Non-Ohmic Conductors: Conductors that do NOT obey Ohm's law ($V$-$I$ graph is non-linear). Examples: diode, transistor, thermistor, filament lamp, vacuum tube, electrolyte at high voltage. Their resistance varies with $V$ or $I$ (dynamic resistance $r_d = dV/dI$).

Temperature Dependence: For metals, resistance increases with temperature: $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$, where $\alpha$ is temperature coefficient of resistance (positive for metals). For semiconductors, $\alpha$ is negative (resistance decreases with temperature).
Filament Lamp: A filament lamp is non-ohmic because its temperature rises as current increases, changing its resistance. Cold resistance is lower than hot resistance.
Diode: A p-n junction diode conducts easily in forward bias (small resistance) and blocks in reverse bias (large resistance). Its $V$-$I$ characteristic is highly non-linear.

Superconductors: Below a critical temperature $T_c$, certain materials exhibit zero electrical resistance ($R = 0$) and expel magnetic fields (Meissner effect). Examples: mercury ($T_c \approx 4.2\text{ K}$), niobium-titanium alloys.
specificConditions: Ohm's Law Validity: Ohm's law $V = IR$ holds only for ohmic materials at constant temperature and other physical conditions. It is NOT a fundamental law of nature but an empirical observation valid for many conductors.

Dynamic vs Static Resistance: For non-ohmic devices, static resistance $R = V/I$ (at a point) differs from dynamic resistance $r_d = dV/dI$ (slope of V-I curve). The dynamic resistance is what matters for small-signal AC analysis.

Temperature Must Be Constant: Ohm's law assumes temperature stays constant. As current flows, Joule heating ($I^2R$) raises temperature, changing resistance — this is why filament lamps are non-ohmic.
keyPoints: Ohm's law: $V = IR$ for ohmic conductors at constant temperature.
Resistance depends on geometry and material: $R = \rho L/A$.
Ohmic conductors have linear V-I graphs; non-ohmic have non-linear graphs.
Examples of non-ohmic: diode, filament lamp, thermistor, transistor.
Temperature coefficient $\alpha$ is positive for metals, negative for semiconductors.
Dynamic resistance $r_d = dV/dI$ differs from static resistance $V/I$ for non-ohmic devices.
importantNotes: Ohm's law is an empirical law, not fundamental — it applies only to ohmic materials at constant physical conditions.
Always distinguish between static resistance ($V/I$) and dynamic resistance ($dV/dI$) for non-ohmic devices.
Temperature changes during current flow can make an ohmic material behave non-ohmically (e.g., filament lamp).
Resistivity $\rho$ is a material property independent of dimensions; resistance $R$ depends on both material and geometry.
examShortTricks: Ohmic = linear V-I graph through origin; Non-ohmic = curved V-I graph.
Use $R = \rho L/A$ — resistance increases with length, decreases with area.
Temperature effect: metals $R \uparrow$ with $T \uparrow$; semiconductors $R \downarrow$ with $T \uparrow$.
For diode in forward bias: resistance is small; reverse bias: resistance is very large.
examNotes: NEB frequently asks to state Ohm's law, define resistance and resistivity, and distinguish ohmic from non-ohmic conductors.
Numerical problems often involve $R = \rho L/A$ with unit conversions (mm² to m²).
V-I graph analysis: slope gives resistance; identify ohmic vs non-ohmic from linearity.
Temperature coefficient problems: use $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$.
examples: A copper wire has resistance $5\,\Omega$ at $20^\circ\text{C}$. If $\alpha = 4.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ K}^{-1}$, find resistance at $50^\circ\text{C}$. Solution: $R_{50} = 5[1 + 4.3\times 10^{-3}(50-20)] = 5[1 + 0.129] = 5.645\,\Omega$.

A wire of length $2\text{ m}$ and cross-section $1\text{ mm}^2$ has resistance $4\,\Omega$. Find its resistivity. Solution: $\rho = RA/L = (4 \times 10^{-6})/2 = 2 \times 10^{-6}\,\Omega\cdot	ext{m}$.
A $12\text{ V}$ battery drives $2\text{ A}$ through a resistor. Find resistance and power. Solution: $R = V/I = 12/2 = 6\,\Omega$; $P = VI = 12 \times 2 = 24\text{ W}$.
A filament lamp draws $0.5\text{ A}$ at $6\text{ V}$ when cold but $0.2\text{ A}$ at $6\text{ V}$ when hot. Cold $R = 12\,\Omega$, hot $R = 30\,\Omega$ — non-ohmic behavior due to temperature change.
practiceQuestions: Q1. State Ohm's law and define resistance. Give its SI unit and dimensional formula.
Q2. Derive the expression $R = \rho L/A$ for the resistance of a uniform conductor.
Q3. Distinguish between ohmic and non-ohmic conductors with examples.
Q4. A wire of length $3\text{ m}$ and area $2\text{ mm}^2$ has resistance $6\,\Omega$. Find its resistivity.
Q5. Explain why a filament lamp is non-ohmic.
Q6. The resistance of a metal is $10\,\Omega$ at $20^\circ\text{C}$ and $12\,\Omega$ at $70^\circ\text{C}$. Find the temperature coefficient of resistance.
Q7. What is dynamic resistance? How does it differ from static resistance for a diode?
practice: Calculate resistance from $V$ and $I$ measurements for ohmic and non-ohmic devices.
Use $R = \rho L/A$ to find resistance, resistivity, length, or area.
Analyze V-I graphs to classify materials as ohmic or non-ohmic.
Apply $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$ for temperature-dependent resistance problems.
Compute power dissipation $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$ in circuits.
Determine dynamic resistance from V-I curve slope for non-ohmic devices.
universalFacts: Ohm's law is an empirical observation, valid for many but not all materials — it is not a fundamental law like conservation of energy.
All materials become non-ohmic at sufficiently high electric fields or temperatures where breakdown occurs.
Superconductors have exactly zero resistance below their critical temperature — a macroscopic quantum phenomenon.
The temperature coefficient of resistance is positive for metals (lattice scattering increases) but negative for semiconductors (more carriers generated).
Semiconductor devices (diodes, transistors) are inherently non-ohmic and form the basis of modern electronics.
confusion: Confusing ohmic with linear: Ohm's law requires linearity AND constant temperature; a heated metal is not ohmic even if its V-I graph looks linear at low currents.
Believing $R = V/I$ is always constant: For non-ohmic devices, $V/I$ changes with operating point; only $dV/dI$ (dynamic resistance) is meaningful locally.
Thinking resistivity changes with dimensions: $\rho$ is an intrinsic material property; only $R$ changes with $L$ and $A$.
Assuming all metals obey Ohm's law perfectly: At very low temperatures or high fields, even metals deviate.
Confusing resistance with resistivity: Resistance depends on geometry; resistivity does not.

mcs.explanation: Resistivity is an intrinsic property of the material and varies with temperature, not dimensions.

mcs.question: A filament lamp is non-ohmic because:
mcs.explanation: As current increases, the filament heats up, changing its resistance — so V/I is not constant.

mcs.question: Dynamic resistance $r_d$ is defined as:
mcs.explanation: Dynamic resistance is the slope of the V-I curve at a point: $r_d = dV/dI$.

summary: Ohm's law ($V = IR$) defines resistance for ohmic conductors with linear V-I characteristics at constant temperature. Resistance depends on geometry and material via $R = \rho L/A$. Non-ohmic conductors (diodes, filament lamps, thermistors) have non-linear V-I graphs where dynamic resistance $dV/dI$ differs from static resistance $V/I$. Temperature coefficient of resistance is positive for metals and negative for semiconductors.
